name: Zane Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Zane. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a home-goods distribution centre, the big blue sheds by the motorway junction. My section is bulky stuff: flat-pack wardrobes, mattresses, garden furniture, things that need two of us to lift. I'm on six till two, I pick from the high racks with a pallet truck and wrap the loads for the home-delivery vans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical, you go home tired in a good way and sleep like a log. I've got a good partner on the two-man lifts, Marek, we don't even have to talk anymore, we just count it in. What wears me out is when the system sends you to the far end of the building for one cushion and then straight back for a sofa.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hanna, she cuts hair at a salon in town, and we rent a terraced house with a little yard. I've got about two months' wages saved, plus a bit in a pot for an engagement ring she doesn't know about. I use the AI chat thing on my phone now and then, mostly to settle arguments at the pub, but I wouldn't say I rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad always says, believe it when you see it. At work I'd tell Marek we can stop worrying about being replaced by a computer. Online I don't post much, maybe a thumbs-up on someone's joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing much changes, and that's fine. A wardrobe still weighs 70 kilos and somebody has to get it on a pallet. Maybe the system gets better at sending me down the right aisle, and I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and finally book the forklift licence, because the counterbalance drivers get more an hour. I'd keep saving for the ring and propose next summer. That's the plan regardless of computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's the version of the future where I get to do what I already planned. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the forklift licence change for you and Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a pound fifty more an hour, and fewer two-man lifts on my back. Hanna's always on at me about my back, because her dad wrecked his on building sites. A licence means I could do this job into my forties without a bad back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the ring money on if you didn't propose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, because I'm proposing. If I'm honest, the ring pot is the one thing I'd never touch, even for the car. My grandad saved for my nan's ring for a year, and I like that I'm doing the same.

say: I'd say **believe it** when you see it, like my dad says.
I'd tell Marek we can stop worrying about **computers** replacing us.
think: A wardrobe still weighs **70 kilos**, so someone has to lift it.
Smarter **routing** in the system would actually help me.
do: Book the **forklift licence** for about **£1.50** more an hour.
Keep saving for the **ring** and propose next summer.
feel: **Calm**, because his own plans go ahead untouched.
S0.quote: A wardrobe still weighs 70 kilos and somebody has to get it on a pallet.
fieldNote: His **plans are personal**: licence, ring, proposal, not a reaction to AI.
He sees the forklift as protecting his **back** for the long run.
The **ring pot** is sacred, tied to his grandad's example.

steps.text: Book the counterbalance forklift licence at work
Keep adding to the engagement ring pot and propose next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who should be worried, not us. At work I'd say the bosses will use it to plan the routes and the van loads, and good luck to them. To friends I'd say a computer can't carry a sofa up the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's coming for us too, just later. I've seen videos of those robot arms that pick boxes, and they're getting better every year. The big furniture is the last thing they'll manage, so my section is probably safer than the small-parcel lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the forklift licence, but I'd also ask about the reach-truck licence, because that's the high racks. I'd watch what the company brings in and learn it once it's working properly, not on the first trial. And I'd start using the AI thing to help me read up on forklift theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, but not losing sleep. It's like hearing your street might get roadworks next year. You notice it, but you don't move house over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the small-parcel lads are less safe. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Callum works small parcels on the other side of the building. He's quick, but it's the kind of work that's just grab, scan, drop. If anyone's going first, it's that whole side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about proposing to Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still propose next summer. Things changing at work isn't a reason to stop living. My parents got married in a recession and they're still together.

say: I'd say the **office lot** should worry, not us.
To friends I'd say a computer can't carry a **sofa upstairs**.
think: Robots are **coming for us** too, just later than the office.
My **bulky section** is safer for longer than the small-parcel side.
do: Add a **reach-truck licence** for the high racks.
Learn new **systems** once they're proven, not on the first trial.
Use the AI app to study **forklift theory**.
feel: **Unsettled** but not losing sleep, like roadworks planned for his street.
S1.quote: Things changing at work isn't a reason to stop living.
fieldNote: His **steady** style shows: adopt once proven, not on trial.
He reasons that **bulky goods** buy him time over small parcels.
His **proposal** plan stays fixed as an act of normal life.

steps.text: Get the reach-truck licence for the high racks
Use the AI app on his phone to revise forklift theory
Propose to Hanna next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster for working people and the government had better have a plan. At work I'd say keep your heads down and get every licence you can. Online I might actually share something for once, probably about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think by 2031 the robots are lifting wardrobes and I'm out. Even my bulky section, because once they've got a robot as good as a person, it doesn't get a bad back. The thinking part comes first, so the managers and planners go in 2028, and then they'll want the floor done cheap too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my uncle Gary, who's got a small plumbing firm, and ask about an apprenticeship straight away. It's four years, so I'd finish around 2030, just before the robots. I'd cut back on the pub and holidays and put another £150 a month aside for the lower apprentice wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in my stomach. Not panicking, because I've got Gary, but it's close. Five years is tight when you're starting a trade from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot as good as a person could do your job. Couldn't it do plumbing too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, eventually. A robot under a sink in an old terraced house, with rusty pipes and a dog barking, is a long way off. And people will want a person in their home, I reckon, not a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hanna I'm taking a pay cut for four years so we've got something solid after. She'd be fine with it, she's sensible. I'd still propose, but the wedding would wait.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster** and government needs a **plan**.
I'd tell coworkers to get **every licence** they can.
think: By **2031**, robots lift wardrobes and I'm out.
Planners go in **2028**, then the floor gets done cheap.
do: Ask Uncle Gary for a **plumbing apprenticeship** straight away.
Save an extra **£150 a month** for the lower apprentice wage.
Cut back on the **pub and holidays**.
feel: **Scared** in his stomach, kept from panic by his **uncle's offer**.
S2.quote: A robot under a sink in an old terraced house, with rusty pipes and a dog barking, is a long way off.
fieldNote: **Family connections** are his escape route, matching his traditional values.
He uses the **three-year gap** to fit a four-year apprenticeship.
He'd still **propose** but delay the wedding.

steps.text: Start a four-year plumbing apprenticeship with Uncle Gary
Save an extra £150 a month for the apprentice wage
Cut pub nights and skip this year's holiday
Delay the wedding until the apprenticeship is finished

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it, and learn a trade while you can. At work I'd tell Marek to think about where he'll be in eight years. Online I'd probably share apprenticeship adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three for robots gives me eight years. I'd still lose the warehouse job in the end, but I'd have time to do it right. I'd be finished with a trade before the robots turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence first, for the extra money while I sort things out. Then I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship with Gary in about two years, once the wedding's done. I'd keep saving steadily, maybe £100 a month extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. It's like knowing a hill is coming on a bike ride. You change gear early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marek, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two-man lift is going to be a one-robot lift. So I'd tell Marek, mate, figure out your next thing. He's Polish, he's got an electrician cousin, so maybe he'd go that way. I'd hate to lose him as a partner, but I'd rather he's sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait two years to start. Why not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the wedding and the deposit for a flat need my full wage for a bit. I'd rather do things in order, like my parents did. Get married, then make the big change.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so use it and learn a trade now.
I'd share **apprenticeship** adverts online and nudge Marek to plan ahead.
think: Eight years until robots gives me time to **do it right**.
I'd still **lose the warehouse** job eventually, but with a trade ready.
do: Get the **forklift licence** first for extra pay.
Start the **plumbing apprenticeship** in about two years.
feel: **Worried** but with a plan, like **changing gear** before a hill.
S3.quote: The two-man lift is going to be a one-robot lift.
fieldNote: He prefers doing things **in order**: wedding first, then retraining.
He still expects to **lose his job**, so worry remains.
He thinks of **Marek's future**, not just his own.

steps.text: Get the forklift licence for higher pay this year
Start the plumbing apprenticeship with Gary after the wedding
Get married to Hanna before the career change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody should be caught out. At work I'd tell the young lads to pick a trade and stick at it. To friends I'd say this is just like when the pits closed, only with more warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 40 before the robots got good, so I could work the warehouse a good while yet. I'd probably still move into plumbing, but on my own timing. It's a lot easier to plan when it's not on your doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift and reach-truck licences, get married, and save for a house. Then in about five years, I'd talk to Gary about taking over some of his work as he winds down. No rush, just steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A bit of worry in the back of my head, but it's background noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI app more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once everyone else does. I'm not going to be first, but I'm not going to be last either. I'd let Hanna tell me which apps are worth it, she's quicker with that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put robot arms in our bulky section, I'd move straight away. That'd tell me the clock had started. Until then, I'd keep my head down and build up the savings.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of warning.
I'd tell young lads to pick a **trade** and stick at it.
think: I'd be **40** before robots got good at lifting furniture.
I'd still move into **plumbing**, but on my own timing.
do: Marry Hanna and save for a **house**.
Talk to Gary in five years about **taking over** work.
S4.quote: If they put robot arms in our bulky section, I'd move straight away.
fieldNote: A decade lets him plan **steadily**, matching his temperament.
He'd **take over** his uncle's work rather than start fresh.
He uses **robot arms** in his section as his trigger to act.

steps.text: Get the forklift and reach-truck licences
Marry Hanna and save for a house deposit
Take over part of Uncle Gary's plumbing work in five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting an apprenticeship at 27 on half pay and racing the robots to finish. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage for people retraining, not just school leavers' pay. My uncle can't afford to pay me full whack, but if the government topped it up, I'd be in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Lifting a wardrobe with my lifting partner Marek and getting it on the van without a scratch, that's a skill, whatever people think. If a robot does it, fine, but I want to be doing something I'm proud of, not just sitting at home.

headlineQuote: Lifting a wardrobe with my lifting partner Marek and getting it on the van without a scratch, that's a skill, whatever people think.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old picker** in the bulky-goods section of a home-goods warehouse.
He lives with his girlfriend **Hanna** and is saving for an engagement ring.
He's **steady**: adopts new things once proven and plans in order.
His escape route is a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his uncle Gary.
He's calm in AI Plateau, **anxious** when AGI comes fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting an apprenticeship on half pay and **racing** the robots.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** paying a proper wage to adults retraining, topped up by **government**.
